segments.title: Compare warships against their intended mission
segments.body: A warship's intended mission gives its gun size, speed, range, and armour their context. Those figures can help a comparison, but they cannot establish how well the design met its navy's needs on their own. The insulation analogy makes this concrete: material suited to the walls can be a poor choice for the floor, while another house or application can change the choice again. Ships from different nations, and different ships within one navy, likewise need to be judged against the roles they were supposed to perform. Compare the intended task with what the ship actually did to assess whether the design worked well.

evidence.note: The opening comparison question, floor-versus-wall insulation analogy, and assessment of intended mission against actual performance.

segments.summary: Compare each ship's intended role with its actual performance, using specifications in the context of its navy's needs.
segments.question: How do you compare ships, including ships from different nations?
segments.answerShort: Assess each ship against its intended mission and role, then ask how well it performed them. Gun size, speed, range, and armour need that operational context.

segments.title: The 1930s Town class and countering surface raiders
segments.body: The 1930s Royal Navy Town-class cruisers were intended to counter surface raiders. The same characteristics that made them suitable for countering surface raiders also made them excellent potential raiders. The suggestion that this second use never occurred to the Royal Navy during design and construction is ironic.

evidence.note: Counter-raider design attributes also suit surface raiding, followed by irony about Royal Navy design intentions.

segments.summary: The Royal Navy's 1930s Town-class cruisers had characteristics suited to both countering surface raiders and raiding themselves.

segments.title: First World War Town cruisers and unexpected merchant raiders
segments.body: The earlier Town-class cruisers had a more passive intended role in scouting, convoy escort, and trade protection. They did go out hunting, although that was not their principal design purpose. The expectation behind the design was that converted merchant cruisers would be too vulnerable to proper warships to make sensible surface raiders. Such ships nevertheless entered that role, and the Towns could hunt them. Their wartime use therefore needs to be distinguished from the tasks and anticipated opponents that shaped the design.

evidence.note: Scouting and trade-protection roles, actual hunting, and the expectation that proper warships would destroy converted merchant raiders.

segments.summary: The earlier Towns went hunting despite their more passive intended role and the expectation that converted merchant raiders would be too vulnerable to use.

segments.title: Why ships with the same class name can demand different comparisons
segments.body: The modern Town class consists of Type 26 anti-submarine frigates. Their ASW role gives them a different mission set from the Town-class cruisers of either world war. Comparing their capabilities directly without accounting for those roles produces a false comparison, even though all share the Town name.

evidence.note: Type 26 ASW frigates have different missions from both generations of Town-class cruisers, making an unqualified capability comparison misleading.

segments.summary: The Town name spans two generations of cruisers and Type 26 anti-submarine frigates whose different missions must shape any capability comparison.

segments.title: Why four super ships may not meet a twelve-ship requirement
segments.body: A ship can have impressive Top Trumps figures and still be a poor answer to its navy's needs. In the hypothetical example, a nation needs twelve ships to cover its positions but can afford only four of an expensive design. Each ship's capabilities therefore have to be weighed against the number the navy needs and can buy. The expensive super ship is not necessarily the best fit when the available budget leaves the required positions uncovered.

evidence.note: A hypothetical navy can afford four expensive ships but needs twelve to cover its positions, so strong individual specifications may not meet its requirements.

segments.summary: A navy needing twelve hulls to cover its positions may be worse served by four expensive super ships, even when each design looks excellent on paper.
